title: Let the plan bend
description: A plan that cannot bend will eventually break; building in flexibility from the start is what makes plans survive real life.

body.heading: Rigidity feels safe and is not
paragraphs: A strict plan — this exact workout, this exact hour, no exceptions — feels strong because it leaves nothing to chance. But it leaves everything to chance: the first disruption has nowhere to go, and a plan with no flex usually fails completely rather than partially.
Flexible plans look softer and last longer. They assume life will interfere, because it will, and they decide in advance how to absorb the interference.

body.heading: Build the bend in advance
paragraphs: For any plan, define three sizes in advance: the full version, the half version, and the two-minute version. A disrupted day then becomes a choosing day, not a failing day. You still did the plan — at the size the day allowed.

Decide also what your plan does about travel, illness and guests, while you are calm. “When I travel, the habit is the two-minute version in the hotel room” is a sentence that saves a great deal of future negotiation.

body.heading: Bending is not drifting
paragraphs: Flexibility has one honest rule: the small version must still be the real thing, just smaller. Two minutes of the actual practice counts. Two minutes of thinking about the practice does not. The bend is in the size, never in the honesty.

Over months, a bending plan produces something a rigid one rarely does: an unbroken thread. The thread matters more than any single session, because the thread is what identity is made of — I am someone who keeps going, at whatever size the day allows.

takeaway: Plan three sizes in advance, and let the day choose which one happens.
